## Ecological Background

*Hymenoscyphus fraxineus* is the causal agent of ash dieback, a non-native fungal disease that has severely affected European ash (*Fraxinus excelsior* L.) populations across Europe over the past three decades (Kowalski & Holdenrieder, 2009; McKinney et al., 2014; Pautasso et al., 2013). Environmental conditions and stand density influence epidemiology, with disease severity declining in low-density stands below 100 stems ha⁻¹ (Skovsgaard et al., 2017; Bakys et al., 2013).

In infested stands, heavy defoliation (50–100% foliage loss) occurs on up to ~30% of mature host trees alongside high sapling mortality (Timmermann et al., 2017), while roughly 1% of ash trees display genetic resistance (Kjær et al., 2012; Wohlmuth et al., 2018).

## Model Implementation

Because quantitative agent population-dynamics data are limited, `ash_dieback` intentionally omits the `BiteBiomass` module and operates directly through `BiteLifeCycle`, `BiteDispersal`, `BiteColonization`, and `BiteImpact`. Spores spread via an inverse power-law dispersal kernel (`maxDistance: 1500` m; Grosdidier et al., 2018), while cell mortality checks whether host density falls below 100 stems ha⁻¹ after year 3.

In `BiteImpact`, 1% host resistance is represented via `treeFilter: 'mod(id, 100)<>42'`, sparing 1% of ash trees from heavy crown defoliation while applying logistic mortality curves to ash saplings.
